q-72303:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-5 & =5(x-1)^{2}-3(y+4)^{2} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{1/3} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y-(-4))^{2}}{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(1,-4,5).$

q-164273:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+4 & =\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{3} \\ z-(-4) & =\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-(-1))^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(3,-1,-4).$

q-164279:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+2 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{(0+3)^{2}}{3} \\ z+2 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{9}{3} \\ z+2 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-3 \\ z+5 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =2(z+5)\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $xz$-plane.

q-35931:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =\frac{4}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =1+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z & =\frac{1}{3}(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $yz$-plane.

q-159579:
The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}).
$$

Since $f(x)=\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3y),$  we have that 

$$
f(x+h,y)=\operatorname{log}⁡(x+h+3y).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+h+3y)-\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3y)}{h}).
$$

q-159589:
The derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by the limit 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{f(x,y+h)-f(x,y)}{h}).
$$

Since $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+2)^{3}},$  we have that 

$$
f(x,y+h)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+h+2)^{3}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={lim}_{h\to 0}[\frac{1}{h}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+h+2)^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+2)^{3}})].
$$

q-159618:
The notation ${f}_{x}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{4}}+6xy) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{4}})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+6y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+6y\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{y}^{4}}+6y\end{aligned}
$$

q-159614:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y)-2\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =5\cdot (0)-2\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

q-159600:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\sqrt{y}-4y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\sqrt{y})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(4y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =2\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-4y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =2\sqrt{y}\cdot (1)-4y\cdot (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{y}-\frac{2y}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,4)} & =2\sqrt{4}-\frac{2\cdot 4}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =4-8 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

q-159587:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\sqrt{x}+\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\sqrt{x}+x{y}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\sqrt{x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{-1}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})+x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{-1}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (2y)+x\cdot (-{y}^{-2}) \\  & =2y\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(4,2)} & =2\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{4}-4\cdot {2}^{-2} \\  & =8-1 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

q-176834:
The general equation of an elliptic cone with center at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}.
$$

To find the center, we rewrite our equation in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-3)^{2}+5(y+2)^{2} & =20(z-1)^{2} \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{1/5} & =\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{1/20} \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{1/5} & =\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{1/20}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic cone that has its center at $(3,-2,1).$

q-94609:
The general equation of an elliptic cone with center at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}.
$$

To find the center, we rewrite our equation in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}+10(y-4)^{2} & =(z-0)^{2} \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{1/10} & =(z-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic cone that has its center at $(1,4,0).$

q-35620:
To find the intersection of the elliptic cone and the plane $z=-2,$ we substitute $z=-2$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+4)^{2}+8{y}^{2} & =12{z}^{2} \\ 3(x+4)^{2}+8{y}^{2} & =12(-2)^{2} \\ 3(x+4)^{2}+8{y}^{2} & =48 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an ellipse with a semi-major axis of length $a=4.$ Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=8.$

q-35596:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{0}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =(z-4)^{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =(z-4)^{2} \\ \pm \frac{y}{2} & =z-4 \\ z & =\pm \frac{y}{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two lines in the $yz$-plane with equations $z=\pm \frac{y}{2}+4.$

q-20966:
The system corresponding to $M$ is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-y+4z=-1 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
x-y+4z=-1
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=-1+y-4z.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1+y-4z \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$, $z$ (free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1+y-4z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+z[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-73953:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3x+5y+2z=1 \\ 0x-2y+4z=3 \\ 0x+0y+0z=10\end{aligned}
$$

Since there are no such numbers $x,y,z$ that form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z=10,$ we can conclude that our system has no solution.
